title: Supreme Court Clears the Way for Mail Ballots Ahead of Midterms
summary:
With voting already underway in some states, the U.S. Supreme Court late Monday lifted a cloud of uncertainty over this year's midterm elections. The court rejected President Donald Trump's push to give the U.S. Postal Service a central role in deciding who could receive a mail ballot. The decision is a win for the status quo: thousands of election offices can now send out mail ballots as they had intended, without complying with new Postal Service rules imposed at the 11th hour.

"Now, we can finally move forward and get back to what we do best: conducting our elections without a dark cloud hanging over us — fairly, openly, for the people, by the people," California Secretary of State Shirley Weber said in a statement.

The case stemmed from an executive order Trump signed in March. His administration developed a plan requiring states to adopt a uniform envelope style for mailed ballots and submit lists of eligible voters to an online portal. The Postal Service could refuse to deliver ballots to states that didn't comply. A whistleblower report warned that the requirements could lead to millions of mail ballots never being sent, disenfranchising many voters during an election that will decide control of Congress.

A tangle of legal challenges and rapid-fire rulings left election officials uncertain. But they agreed on one thing: introducing such massive changes so close to a general election would be chaotic and nearly impossible in a country where roughly a third of voters use mail ballots. The concern was particularly acute in eight states where voters cast ballots almost entirely by mail: California, Colorado, Hawaii, Nevada, Oregon, Utah, Vermont and Washington.

Lower courts had blocked the administration from implementing its rules. The Supreme Court rejected its attempt to stay those decisions, even as three justices — Samuel Alito, Brett Kavanaugh and Clarence Thomas — expressed willingness to let Trump carry out his plan. Yet a majority noted the administration was "unlikely to succeed on the merits." "This provides voters and elections officials with the certainty they need ahead of a major, federal election," said Oregon Secretary of State Tobias Read. "Presidents don't run elections, the people do."
why_it_matters: The rules for getting and returning a mail ballot are decided by courts and election offices, not just by politicians — and choices made now can decide whether millions of Americans, including your own family, can actually vote in November and in every future election.

questions.question: What did the Supreme Court reject in its late-Monday decision?
options: A whistleblower's report about election fraud
President Trump's push to give the Postal Service a central role in deciding who could receive a mail ballot
A request to delay the midterm elections
California's plan to mail ballots to every voter
questions.correct_answer: President Trump's push to give the Postal Service a central role in deciding who could receive a mail ballot

questions.question: What did the administration's March executive order require states to do?
options: Use only the Postal Service rather than private carriers
Count all mail ballots by hand
Print every ballot in two languages
Adopt a uniform envelope style for mailed ballots and submit lists of eligible voters to an online portal
questions.correct_answer: Adopt a uniform envelope style for mailed ballots and submit lists of eligible voters to an online portal

questions.question: How many states were described as holding elections almost entirely by mail?
options: Five
Three
Twelve
Eight

questions.question: Which three justices expressed willingness to let Trump carry out his plan?
options: Brett Kavanaugh, Clarence Thomas and Tobias Read
Shirley Weber, Tobias Read and Elizabeth Warren
Samuel Alito, Brett Kavanaugh and Clarence Thomas
Samuel Alito, Shirley Weber and Tobias Read
questions.correct_answer: Samuel Alito, Brett Kavanaugh and Clarence Thomas

questions.question: Why did election officials say the new requirements would be a problem?
options: They would end early in-person voting
They would ban mail ballots completely
Introducing massive changes so close to a general election would be chaotic and nearly impossible
They would cost too much money
questions.correct_answer: Introducing massive changes so close to a general election would be chaotic and nearly impossible

questions.question: What did Oregon Secretary of State Tobias Read say?
options: 'The court has failed the American people.'
'Mail voting should be abolished.'
'We will comply with the Postal Service rules.'
'Presidents don't run elections, the people do.'
questions.correct_answer: 'Presidents don't run elections, the people do.'

background_read: The U.S. Supreme Court is the country's highest court; its nine justices — including Samuel Alito, Brett Kavanaugh and Clarence Thomas — are appointed for life and have the final say on whether laws and executive actions can stand.

In the United States, elections are run by state and local officials rather than by the president or by Washington, which is why a federal agency like the U.S. Postal Service setting rules for mail ballots triggered such a fight.

Mail voting has grown for decades, and a handful of states such as Oregon and Washington have held almost all of their elections by post for years; Shirley Weber, California's secretary of state, is the official in charge of running elections in the biggest of those states.
The Postal Service's role became especially controversial in 2020, when the pandemic pushed record numbers of Americans to vote by mail and courts had to settle disputes over delivery times.

Judges often apply what lawyers call the 'Purcell principle' — the idea that courts should avoid changing election rules too close to voting day, because last-minute confusion can keep people from voting.

perspectives.perspective: Positive — election officials and mail-voting states
perspectives.description: Secretaries of state and county election offices see the ruling as a win: they can print and send ballots on schedule, and voters get certainty instead of a 'dark cloud' hanging over the election. States where nearly everyone votes by mail say they could not have rebuilt their systems in weeks.

perspectives.perspective: Critical — the administration and the dissenting justices
perspectives.description: The administration argues the Postal Service has a legitimate role in protecting ballot security, and that courts should not block a president's election-integrity measures before they are even tried. The three dissenting justices signalled they would have let the plan proceed while the legal case continued.

perspectives.perspective: Neutral / analytical — the long tug-of-war over election rules
perspectives.description: Historically, states and counties run elections while the federal government sets only some national standards, so this is the latest round in a decades-old fight over who controls the mechanics of voting. Courts have repeatedly warned that changing procedures close to election day creates confusion that harms voters of every party.

The underlying case is not over, and similar late rule changes are likely to be challenged again in future elections. Congress could eventually write clearer national standards for mail ballots, but until then the boundaries will keep being drawn by judges, often on very short timelines.
